comments.content: Just to clarify, everyone should already be able to access the conference link and make a submission. When you access the link, your console should look like the below image. Then, you can click "Create new submission" to submit your final project draft. Only one member of each group needs to make a submission; when doing so, that one member should add the emails of all their collaborators (using your @berkeley.edu email). Meanwhile, you should have also received invitations to be peer reviewers. Please accept the invitation as soon as possible; this time, every member of each group should should accept their own invitation. Once you accept, you should have the option to switch roles between "Author" and "Reviewer" via the navigation bar at the top (though the "Reviewer" dashboard will be empty initially). After all submission are in, we will assign project drafts for each of you to review and provide feedback on. We are still getting used to this conference submission system, so if any issues arise please ask them in this thread and I will try to resolve them.

comments.content:
Hey everybody,The Draft Project Report is due tomorrow, and with that, I wanted to share a prompt that worked very good for critiquing the Project Paper. Personally, my team and I used it on ChatGPT 5.1, but I'm assuming similar results may be achieved on any other LLM service. Sharing it below so that everybody can get critiques for their papers before submitting!
You are a peer reviewer for a top-tier machine learning conference (e.g., NeurIPS/ICLR/ICML).
Your task is to provide a rigorous, critical, and highly specific review of my paper.
Your critique should follow the standards of senior reviewers.

Do the following:

1. Identify Major Strengths and Contributions
    •    What are the core contributions?
    •    Are they novel, meaningful, and well-supported?
    •    How clearly are they articulated?

⸻

2. Identify Major Weaknesses

Be specific, concrete, and technical. For each weakness:
    •    Quote or reference the part of the text where the issue appears.
    •    Explain why it is a weakness in the context of ML optimization literature.
    •    Propose precise revisions or experiments that would fix the weakness.

Categories to consider:
    •    Conceptual clarity
    •    Mathematical rigor
    •    Missing related work
    •    Weak experimental methodology
    •    Unsupported claims
    •    Lack of ablations
    •    Insufficient theoretical grounding
    •    Overclaiming
    •    Misinterpretation of cited work
    •    Dataset/benchmark choice
    •    Reproducibility
    •    Insufficient baselines

⸻

3. Assess Writing Quality

Evaluate:
    •    the structure and flow
    •    clarity of arguments
    •    consistency of notation
    •    ambiguity or vagueness
    •    overuse of jargon
Then provide suggestions for clearer exposition.

⸻

4. Evaluate Technical Correctness

Check:
    •    whether definitions and equations are precise
    •    whether the proposed method is correctly derived
    •    whether theoretical statements are logically supported
    •    whether claims match what is actually proven/demonstrated

For any issue: explain exactly what is incorrect or underspecified, and how to correct it.

⸻

5. Evaluate Experimental Methodology

Critique:
    •    model configurations
    •    baselines (missing or insufficient)
    •    hyperparameter tuning fairness
    •    ablation completeness
    •    significance of results
    •    statistical robustness
    •    choice of dataset and its limitations

Then suggest:
    •    additional ablations
    •    stronger baselines
    •    larger-scale experiments
    •    stress-test tasks
    •    diagnostic plots

⸻

6. Provide a Reproducibility Score

Rate on a 1–10 scale:
    •    How easy would it be for another researcher to replicate the work?
Explain what is missing (e.g., training details, seed fixes, optimizer settings, exact LR schedules).

⸻

7. Give an Overall Score and Recommendation

Using standard conference scoring:
    •    8–10: Strong accept
    •    6–7: Weak accept
    •    4–5: Borderline
    •    2–3: Weak reject
    •    1: Strong reject

Explain the reasoning behind your score and outline what revisions would be necessary for acceptance.

⸻

8. Provide a Line-Edit Pass (Optional but Helpful)

Offer:
    •    rephrasings of unclear sentences
    •    improved transitions
    •    concise rewrites of long paragraphs
    •    notation cleanup suggestions

⸻

Your critique must be:
    •    brutally honest
    •    detailed (at least 800–1200 words)
    •    objective and professional
    •    technically grounded
    •    constructive, offering actionable improvements

⸻

comments.content:
Hey, I'm sure a lot of people are proofreading right now, and if you want especially hard advice, try taking a look using this adversarial prompt: 
Role:
 You are an adversarial, skeptical, senior Area Chair (AC) at a top-tier ML conference (NeurIPS/ICML).
 Your job is not to be polite. Your job is to stress-test the paper until it breaks.
 Assume the authors are overselling their work unless proven otherwise.
 No praise. No diplomacy. Maximum rigor. Maximum skepticism.
 
Task:
 Perform a full Red Team Audit of the paper below.
 Do NOT summarize the paper.
Your job is to uncover flaws, weak assumptions, missing experiments, logical gaps, and oversold claims.
Your analysis must attack the work from five distinct angles, described below.

1. “So What?” / Motivation Stress Test

For this section, do the following:
Attack the main premise: Argue why the stated problem may not matter or may already be solved.

Critique the claimed gap: Explain why the “gap” the authors claim may be trivial, artificial, or mischaracterized.

Check for straw-man baselines: Identify where baselines or prior work may be misrepresented or intentionally weakened.

Goal: Argue why this paper might be fundamentally unnecessary.

2. “House of Cards” Logic Audit
Perform a chain-of-logic stress test:

Trace every major argument from Abstract to Method to Experiments to Conclusion. Identify where the logic breaks.

Find the “Magic Steps”: Any unjustified assumption, heuristic, hyperparameter, or derivation hand-wave. Flag these explicitly as MAGIC STEP #1, MAGIC STEP #2, etc.

Claim–Evidence Mapping:

List all major claims in the Introduction.

For each claim, state whether the Experiments section actually proves it—or only a weaker proxy.

Goal: Show how the paper overclaims relative to evidence.

3. Experimental Rigor / Cherry-Picking Detection
Assume the authors are gaming the experiments. Attack the empirical setup:
Hyperparameter Skepticism: Identify where the authors may have tuned their method more aggressively than baselines.

Dataset Bias: Critique dataset selection; argue why these datasets are “easy mode” for this method and propose a “hard mode” dataset that might break it.

Missing Critical Ablations: Identify the one key component that the authors should ablate but did not, and argue why its absence is suspicious.

Goal: Demonstrate that the empirical section may be cherry-picked or engineered for success.

4. Lazy Reviewer Simulation
Write:
A paragraph describing what a lazy reviewer will misunderstand, misread, or incorrectly assume about this paper.

A single sentence that the authors should add to the Abstract/Intro to prevent that misunderstanding.

Goal: Expose ambiguity and poor framing that will hurt the paper.

5. Rejection Pre-Mortem
Write the rejection as if you are the AC informing the authors of their decision:
One ruthless sentence summarizing why the paper is rejected.

A concise rejection notice (3–5 sentences).
A rebuttal strategy the authors should use to counter this rejection if they want to salvage the paper.

Tone:
 Brutally honest. Unforgiving. Academic but adversarial.
 Do not offer praise or encouragement.
 Do not hedge (“might”, “could”, “perhaps”).
 Speak with full confidence.
Format Requirements:
 Use bold section headers matching the structure above.
 No bullet-point summaries of the paper.
 Do not dilute criticism.

comments.content:
I've used Chain of Thought prompting to get a prompt that I used to get an LLM to review our project. Here is the prompt
Provide detailed, expert feedback on my neural networks project report, following these instructions:

1. Evaluate the report strictly according to NeurIPS paper standards (see 2015 style guidelines). Base your feedback ONLY on neural-network–relevant criteria. Do NOT require or evaluate novelty — novelty is NOT a requirement for this project.

2. Assess whether the core paper (5-10 pages) clearly tells a coherent main story about the project, including situating it within relevant NN literature, having key figures, and providing a concise abstract.

3. Critically evaluate the literature review:
   - Does it clearly position the work within the NN literature?
   - Does it include 2-3+ pages of discussion on related work exploring similar NN ideas?
   - Is it crisp, detailed, and technically accurate?

4. Evaluate the methods section:
   - Is it self-contained, mathematically correct, and unambiguous?
   - Are diagrams, pseudocode, or code snippets clear and fully labeled?
   - Are in-progress parts clearly marked?

5. Assess experiments and results:
   - Are hyperparameters clearly tabulated with explanations for how and why they were chosen?
   - Are experiments controlled and isolating one change at a time?
   - Are critical NN components (architectures, training procedures, losses, optimization steps) thoroughly described?

6. Evaluate figures and plots:
   - Are plots NN-relevant and properly labeled (axes, scales, units)?
   - Are error bars used when appropriate, and is the method for computing them explained?
   - Are training curves, validation metrics, and comparative baselines presented and analyzed?

7. Evaluate replicability and GitHub readiness:
   - Does the paper clearly explain how plots/tables/results can be reproduced?
   - Is dataset handling properly described (fetching, preprocessing, splits)?
   - If custom datasets are used, is justification provided?

8. Evaluate overall correctness:
   - Identify missing controls, confounders, or weak experimental design choices.
   - Identify unclear assumptions or missing mathematical details.
   - Point out where the narrative of the paper is inconsistent with results.

9. Evaluate conceptual clarity:
   - Is the key idea well-motivated and tied to prior NN work, regardless of novelty?
   - Are limitations and failure modes clearly discussed?
   - Are any techniques outside course scope explained clearly for peers?

10. Provide actionable, specific, technically grounded feedback:
    - What should be added, removed, clarified, or expanded?
    - What NN-specific issues should be improved (architecture choices, training procedure, baselines, evaluation)?

Return feedback in structured sections with explicit references to the above criteria. Do not give generic writing advice; keep all feedback focused on neural networks and research-paper quality.

comments.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>I generally like these prompts, but you all should try to make sure that your feedback is aimed at improving the rigor and completeness of the work. <bold>Technical novelty is not required in the project</bold>. And I wouldn't want anyone to essentially be put in a position to inadvertently shape the writing to try to satisfy this nonexistent criteria.</paragraph><paragraph>What we want is systematic and thorough investigation. As we have said, the basic perspective on the project is to thoroughly investigate a question carefully that could result from Paper A being applied to the setting of Paper B. It's fine if there's a clear default answer for what should or would likely happen. It's fine if the thorough investigation confirms that. A conference might not consider that novel, but we don't care. What matters is demonstrating your mastery of the material and the ability to apply/use/adapt it systematically. </paragraph></document>

I generally like these prompts, but you all should try to make sure that your feedback is aimed at improving the rigor and completeness of the work. Technical novelty is not required in the project. And I wouldn't want anyone to essentially be put in a position to inadvertently shape the writing to try to satisfy this nonexistent criteria.

What we want is systematic and thorough investigation. As we have said, the basic perspective on the project is to thoroughly investigate a question carefully that could result from Paper A being applied to the setting of Paper B. It's fine if there's a clear default answer for what should or would likely happen. It's fine if the thorough investigation confirms that. A conference might not consider that novel, but we don't care. What matters is demonstrating your mastery of the material and the ability to apply/use/adapt it systematically.

comments.content: Sorry I didn't see this post earlier. But if you want a bit of an easier way to get feedback on your project code regardless of the size of your codebase, you can also use https://gitingest.com to collapse your entire code into one LLM readable file and then prompt any LLM with that file to test for bugs, feedback on code structure improvements, etc. Your code has to be in a public repository for this to work. If not, you can also install gitingest via pip and then go to your local project repository and do gitingest . it will create a similar LLM readable text file.I found this useful especially when I was hitting limits with Claude Code or Antigravity. It would also be useful if you have access to extended limit Pro versions of LLMs but not to those versions on cursor or any other similar platform.

Hi everyone,I designed a prompt to specifically check if our paper is telling a coherent story rather than trying to "fake" novelty.Prompt: 
Role: You are a supportive but rigorous Research Mentor helping a student polish a NeurIPS-style project report. Your goal is NOT to reject the paper, but to ensure it meets the specific pedagogical goals of a "systematic investigation" project.
Context: The authors are students. They are NOT required to have ground breaking technical novelty (SOTA results). Instead, they are required to demonstrate:
1. Systematic Investigation: Controlled experiments and clear baselines
2. Narrative Consistency: The abstract, intro, and conclusion must tell the exact same coherent story.
3. Replicability: Hyperparameters must be justified.
Task: specific feedback on the draft report based on the following 2 areas.
1. The Fake Novelty Audit (Crucial) Review the Introduction and Abstract. Are the authors trying too hard to sound "novel"?
* Check: Do they use buzzwords to mask a simple application?
* Action: If they are overselling, suggest specific re-phrasings that pivot the tone from "We created a novel architecture..." to "We systematically investigated the application of X on Y…”.
2. Narrative Thread Consistency
* Check: Does the Conclusion actually answer the specific question posed in the Introduction?
* Check: Do the plots visually support the text claims? (eg, If the text says Model A converges faster, does the plot actually show that clearly, or is the scale ambiguous?)
Output Format: Please provide the feedback in bullet points under the 2 headers above. Be constructive and specific (quote the text).

2. Narrative Thread Consistency
* Check: Does the Conclusion actually answer the specific question posed in the Introduction?
* Check: Do the plots visually support the text claims? (eg, If the text says Model A converges faster, does the plot actually show that clearly, or is the scale ambiguous?)
Output Format: Please provide the feedback in bullet points under the 2 headers above. Be constructive and specific (quote the text).

Hi Everyone,

I've put together some helpful prompts based on the review process to polish my group's final report. I hope you find them helpful.

1. Contributions Summary

"Help me draft a more concise and impactful summary of the paper's main contributions for the abstract, ensuring the main contributions are immediately clear."

2. Quality of Writing/Notation

"Review the 'Methodology' section for clarity and consistency. Point out any undefined notation or instances where the English language could be made more precise and formal."

3. Hypothesis & Validation

"Help me strengthen my Hypotheses or Research questions by ensuring that the experimental results directly address each stated hypothesis and that the baselines are clearly justified as sensible comparisons."

4. Literature Review

"Suggest ways to broaden the literature review by integrating a discussion on closely related but distinct methodologies (Topic X) and explicitly contrasting our work with them to better position our contribution."

5. Hyperparameters/Architecture

"Review the 'Implementation Details' section. Suggest how to better motivate our architectural choices and hyperparameter settings, either by citing literature or by briefly explaining the rationale behind them."

6. Experimental Setup Quality

"Help me critically evaluate the experiments and ablations. Identify any instances where the experiment design might be changing multiple variables simultaneously and propose a single, clear ablation study to isolate a specific effect, if not already present."

7. Results Quality (Plots/Analysis)

"Critique the quality of the quantitative results and figures. Ensure that all figures have been explained in the text, include clearly labeled axes and appropriate error bars (if needed), and that the analysis emphasizes interpretable metrics."

Hi everyone, I made a prompt that acts as a "Meta-Reviewer" that takes your Draft + the Peer Reviews you received and outputs a prioritized Revision Checklist for the final report.

Prompt
Role: You are a Senior Editor for a machine learning conference. Your goal is to guide the authors (students) in revising their project report based on peer feedback.

Inputs:

The Current Draft: [Paste Draft Here]

Peer Reviews Received: [Paste all Reviewer Comments Here]

Context: This is a course project where "Technical Novelty" is NOT required. The primary goal is a "Systematic Investigation" (controlled experiments, clear baselines, narrative consistency).

Task: Analyze the reviews and the draft to produce a Final Revision Plan.

Output 1: Conflict Resolution

Identify any conflicting feedback between reviewers (e.g., Reviewer A says "Shorten section X", Reviewer B says "Expand section X").

Recommend which reviewer to follow based on which advice better aligns with the "Systematic Investigation" rubric.

Output 2: The "Scope Creep" Guard

Flag any reviewer suggestions that would require massive new engineering work (e.g., "Implement this totally different SOTA model") which might be out of scope for the remaining time.

Suggest a way to address these via text/analysis (e.g., "Add to Future Work section") rather than new code.

Output 3: Prioritized Checklist

Critical Fixes: (Flaws in logic, misleading plots, missing baselines).

Narrative Fixes: (Clarifying the story, fixing abstract-conclusion alignment).

Low-Hanging Fruit: (Typos, notation cleanup, formatting).

Output 4: Response Strategy

Draft a brief "Response to Reviewers" strategy for the major points, explaining how we fixed them (or why we didn't).
